# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The evolution of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been marked by successive technological advances, from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents (BMS) and drug-eluting stents (DES) [1]. Despite the clinical success of contemporary DES, permanent metallic implants are associated with persistent limitations, including chronic vessel caging, impaired vasomotion, neoatherosclerosis, and the ongoing risk of very late stent thrombosis [2,3]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to provide transient mechanical support during vessel healing and subsequently dissolve, theoretically restoring normal vascular physiology and eliminating the long-term sequelae of permanent implants [4]. This review summarizes the rationale, clinical evidence, and current status of BVS in PCI.

## Concept and Device Design

The central premise of BVS is "leaving nothing behind." After scaffolding the vessel during the critical period of healing, the device is intended to fully resorb, permitting restoration of vasomotor tone, late lumen enlargement, and adaptive remodeling [4,5]. The most extensively studied device was the Absorb everolimus-eluting bioresorbable vascular scaffold (Abbott Vascular), composed of a poly-L-lactide backbone with a poly-D,L-lactide coating eluting everolimus [6]. Degradation occurs through hydrolysis of ester bonds, with complete resorption over approximately two to three years [5]. Other devices, including the magnesium-based Magmaris scaffold, employed bioresorbable metallic alloys [7].

## Early Clinical Evidence

The first-in-man ABSORB cohort A study demonstrated feasibility and acceptable short-term outcomes, with serial imaging showing scaffold resorption and recovery of vasomotion [8,9]. The ABSORB cohort B study extended these observations, confirming late luminal preservation and bioresorption on optical coherence tomography and intravascular ultrasound [10]. These encouraging findings generated substantial enthusiasm, positioning BVS as a potential paradigm shift in interventional cardiology [4].

## Randomized Trials and Meta-Analyses

The pivotal ABSORB II, ABSORB III, ABSORB Japan, and ABSORB China trials compared the Absorb BVS with the Xience cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stent [11–14]. ABSORB III, the largest trial, demonstrated non-inferiority for target lesion failure at one year, supporting US regulatory approval [12]. However, longer-term follow-up revealed concerning signals. ABSORB II failed to meet its co-primary endpoints, showing no superiority in vasomotion and worse late lumen loss [11]. Pooled analyses and meta-analyses consistently identified higher rates of device-oriented adverse events and scaffold thrombosis, particularly between one and three years [15–17]. The AIDA trial similarly reported increased definite or probable scaffold thrombosis with Absorb compared with Xience [18]. A patient-level meta-analysis confirmed an excess of target lesion failure and very late scaffold thrombosis [19].

## Mechanisms of Failure

Several mechanisms underlie BVS-related events. The thick struts (approximately 150 µm) increased thrombogenicity and impaired flow, while incomplete lesion preparation and scaffold underexpansion contributed to malapposition [20,21]. Late scaffold discontinuity during resorption created intraluminal dismantling, a substrate for late thrombosis identified on intravascular imaging [22,23]. Recognition of these issues prompted refinement of implantation technique, encapsulated in the "PSP" (predilatation, sizing, post-dilatation) approach, which improved outcomes in observational registries [24,25].

## Real-World Registries and Technique Optimization

Large registries such as GHOST-EU and the ABSORB registries documented real-world performance, highlighting elevated early and late thrombosis rates, especially in small vessels and complex lesions [26,27]. Optimized implantation with meticulous vessel preparation, accurate sizing, and aggressive post-dilatation reduced adverse events, underscoring the importance of operator technique and lesion selection [24,28].

## Current Status and Future Directions

Owing to the unfavorable risk profile and commercial considerations, Abbott withdrew the Absorb BVS from the market in 2017 [29]. Nevertheless, the concept of bioresorbable technology remains scientifically compelling. Next-generation scaffolds with thinner struts, improved polymers, and faster resorption are under investigation, alongside magnesium-based devices that have shown promising early results [7,30]. Lessons learned regarding strut thickness, mechanical integrity, patient selection, and implantation technique are guiding this development [30].

## Conclusion

BVS represented an ambitious effort to overcome the limitations of permanent metallic stents by providing temporary scaffolding followed by complete resorption. Although early studies were encouraging, randomized trials and meta-analyses revealed increased rates of device-related events and scaffold thrombosis with first-generation devices, leading to market withdrawal [16,19,29]. The clinical trajectory of BVS illustrates both the promise and the challenges of disruptive interventional technologies. Refined device design and rigorous technique optimization may yet allow bioresorbable scaffolds to fulfill their original promise in selected patients [30].
